7. Rule 26(e) authorizes the court to sanction a party’s failure to supplement a disclosure or response. The significant question in many disputes
about supplementation is whether the duty was triggered. In Poitra v. School District No. 1 in the County of Denver, 311 F.R.D. 659 (D.Colo. 2015),
plaintiff failed to include a witness in the initial Rule 26(a)(1) disclosures or in any written supplemental disclosure prior to the final pretrial
conference. Two months before trial, defendant moved to strike the witness and for sanctions. Plaintiff defended by pointing to specific deposition
testimony from the witness as satisfying the supplementation obligation.
Rule 26(e) must be construed and applied against the backdrop of the very specific requirements set forth in Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(i). Indeed, the
elements of Rule 26(e) are quite clear. First, to trigger the duty to supplement, a party’s initial disclosures must, in some respect, be
incomplete or incorrect. Here, that element is not in dispute * * *. Second, Rule 26(e)(1)(A) requires that supplemental disclosures occur “in
a timely manner.” * * * And finally, a reasonable interpretation of Rule 26(e)(1)(A) and its reference to “incomplete or incorrect”
disclosures presumes that the “additional or corrective information . . . otherwise made known . . . during the discovery process” will
provide the functional equivalent of the information required under Rule 26(a)(1)(A). * * *
* * *
While discovery is, by necessity, an iterative process, Plaintiff’s interpretation of the “otherwise made known” phrase has the potential to
convert the Rule 26(e) supplementation requirement into a “whack-a-mole” game. * * * Constrained by the numerical limit on depositions
imposed under Rule 30(a)(2) and by proportionality factors expressly incorporated in Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1), opposing counsel is
confronted with a real dilemma if the mere mention of an individual’s name during a deposition discharges a party’s disclosure and
supplementation obligations. A risk-averse party must either expend time and money taking a deposition that could prove worthless, or risk
surprise at trial. * * *
* * *
* * * [I]t it is the practical effect of counsel’s interpretation of Rule 26(e) that is most troubling. Rule 26(a)(1) and (e)(1) impose an
affirmative obligation to provide disclosures that are complete and correct as of the time they are made. The importance of that disclosure
obligation is reflected in the certification requirement imposed on counsel under Rule 26(g). A passing and perhaps oblique reference to an
